intro: Snakes are long, legless reptiles that slither, swim and even climb trees. Some are tiny and some are enormous, and most are completely harmless to people. Let's slither into some super snake facts!

quick.Food: Mice, birds, eggs, frogs, fish and insects
quick.Size: From about 4 inches (10 cm) to over 20 feet (6 m) long
quick.Life span: Often 10 to 30 years, depending on the kind

facts: There are more than 3,900 kinds of snakes.
Snakes live on every continent except Antarctica.
Snakes are reptiles, which means they are cold-blooded and covered in scales.
Snakes warm up by lying in the sun and cool down in the shade.
Snakes don't have eyelids. A clear scale covers and protects each eye.
Snakes smell with their tongues! They flick them out to collect smells from the air.
Snakes don't have outside ears, but they can feel vibrations through the ground.
Snakes shed their whole skin as they grow, often in one long piece.
Snakes swallow their food whole because they can't chew.
Stretchy jaws let snakes swallow animals bigger than their heads.
After a big meal, some snakes don't need to eat again for weeks.
Most snakes are not venomous, and many are harmless to people.
Venomous snakes use special teeth called fangs.
Pythons and boas squeeze their food instead of using venom.
The reticulated python is the longest snake and can grow over 20 feet (6 m).
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
The Barbados threadsnake is one of the smallest snakes and is only about 4 inches (10 cm) long.
Some snakes lay eggs, and others give birth to live babies.
Baby snakes are called snakelets or hatchlings.
Rattlesnakes shake the rattle on their tails to warn others to stay away.
Pit vipers can sense the body heat of animals, even in the dark.
Some snakes can climb trees, and a few can even glide from branch to branch!
Sea snakes spend almost their whole lives in the ocean.
Snakes help farmers by eating mice and rats that damage crops.
If you see a snake outside, the best thing to do is give it space and let a grown-up know.
faq: How do snakes move without legs?
Snakes use strong muscles and belly scales that grip the ground. They push against bumps, curve side to side and stretch and bunch up to move along.
Are all snakes dangerous?
No. Most snakes are not venomous and are harmless to people. Still, it's always best to leave wild snakes alone and tell a grown-up.
Why do snakes flick their tongues?
Snakes smell with their tongues. They flick them to collect scents, then touch the tongue to a special smell organ in the roof of their mouth.
What is the biggest snake?
The reticulated python is the longest snake, growing over 20 feet. The green anaconda is the heaviest.

intro: Spiders are eight-legged creatures that spin silk, build amazing webs and help keep bugs under control. They might look a little spooky, but most spiders are helpful friends. Let's creep into some cool spider facts!

quick.Home: Almost everywhere on land, on every continent except Antarctica
quick.Size: From smaller than a pinhead to about 11 inches (28 cm) across with legs
quick.Life span: About 1 to 2 years for most kinds; some tarantulas live 20 years or more

facts: Spiders are not insects. They are arachnids.
Insects have six legs, but spiders have eight.
There are about 50,000 known kinds of spiders.
Most spiders have eight eyes, but some have six, four, two or even none.
All spiders can make silk.
Pound for pound, spider silk can be stronger than steel.
Spiders spin silk from body parts called spinnerets at the end of their bodies.
Not all spiders build webs. Some hunt, jump or hide and wait.
Orb-weaver spiders build round, wheel-shaped webs.
Many orb-weavers build a brand new web every day.
Spiders have tiny hairs on their legs that feel vibrations, so they know when something lands in their web.
Spiders don't get stuck in their own webs because they walk on special non-sticky threads.
Jumping spiders can leap many times the length of their own bodies.
Jumping spiders have big front eyes and great eyesight.
Baby spiders are called spiderlings.
Some baby spiders travel by floating through the air on silk threads. This is called ballooning.
Mother wolf spiders carry their babies on their backs.
The Goliath birdeater is one of the biggest spiders, with legs about 11 inches (28 cm) across.
Some spiders are smaller than the head of a pin.
Spiders eat lots of insects, like flies and mosquitoes, which helps people.
Tarantulas are big, hairy spiders that can live for many years.
Most spiders are harmless to people, and only a few are dangerous.
Spiders have been on Earth for hundreds of millions of years.
A fear of spiders is called arachnophobia.
Spiders are a favorite in nursery rhymes, like the Itsy Bitsy Spider who climbs up the water spout!
faq: Is a spider an insect?
No. Spiders are arachnids. Insects have six legs and three body parts, while spiders have eight legs and two body parts.
How do spiders make webs?
Spiders make silk inside their bodies and pull it out of spinnerets. They connect threads in patterns to make webs that catch insects.
Why don't spiders stick to their own webs?
Spiders know which threads are sticky and walk on the dry ones. They also step carefully, using special hooked claws on their feet.
Are spiders dangerous?
Most spiders are harmless and helpful because they eat pests. Only a few spiders can hurt people, so it's best not to touch wild spiders.

intro: Hedgehogs are small, spiky animals that roll into a prickly ball when they feel scared. They snuffle around at night looking for bugs to eat. Let's roll into some fun hedgehog facts!

quick.Home: Gardens, hedges, woods and grasslands in Europe, Asia and Africa
quick.Food: Beetles, caterpillars, worms and other bugs
quick.Size: About 5 to 12 inches (13 to 30 cm) long
quick.Life span: About 2 to 5 years in the wild

facts: There are 17 kinds of hedgehogs.
Wild hedgehogs live in Europe, Asia and Africa, but not in the Americas.
A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines on its back.
Hedgehog spines are hollow hairs made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
Hedgehog spines aren't poisonous, and hedgehogs can't shoot them.
When scared, a hedgehog rolls into a tight, spiky ball.
Hedgehogs got their name because they like to live in hedges and make snorting, pig-like sounds.
Hedgehogs are nocturnal, which means they are most active at night.
Hedgehogs eat beetles, caterpillars, worms, slugs and other small creatures.
Gardeners like hedgehogs because they eat bugs that damage plants.
Hedgehogs have a great sense of smell and hearing, but not very good eyesight.
A hedgehog can walk a mile or more in one night looking for food.
Some hedgehogs hibernate in winter, sleeping in cozy nests of leaves.
Baby hedgehogs are called hoglets.
Hoglets are born with soft spines under their skin that pop out a few hours after birth.
A group of hedgehogs is called an array.
Hedgehogs sometimes lick strange smells and spread foamy spit on their spines. This is called self-anointing.
Hedgehogs can swim and climb.
Hedgehogs make snuffling, grunting and huffing sounds.
The African pygmy hedgehog is a popular kind of pet hedgehog.
Hedgehogs have been around for millions of years.
Hedgehogs shouldn't drink milk because it gives them tummy aches.
Leaving a small gap in a garden fence makes a 'hedgehog highway' so they can travel safely.
Hedgehogs are mostly loners and like to live on their own.
Some hedgehogs have spines that are white, brown or striped with both.
faq: Why do hedgehogs have spikes?
Their spines protect them. When a hedgehog is scared, it curls into a ball so predators only see a prickly ball of spikes.
What do hedgehogs eat?
Hedgehogs mostly eat insects and other small creatures, like beetles, caterpillars, worms and slugs.
What is a baby hedgehog called?
A baby hedgehog is called a hoglet.
Are hedgehogs nocturnal?
Yes. Hedgehogs sleep during the day and come out at night to search for food.

intro: Sea otters are playful ocean animals with the thickest fur in the world. They float on their backs, use rocks as tools and sometimes hold hands while they sleep! Let's float into some sweet sea otter facts!

quick.Home: Coastal waters of the North Pacific Ocean
quick.Food: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels and fish

facts: Sea otters live in the North Pacific Ocean, along the coasts of North America and Asia.
Sea otters are one of the smallest marine mammals.
Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal, with up to about a million hairs per square inch.
Unlike seals and whales, sea otters don't have a layer of blubber. Their fur keeps them warm.
Sea otters spend lots of time grooming to keep their fur clean and fluffy.
Sea otters spend most of their lives in the water.
Sea otters float on their backs to eat, rest and groom.
Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open clams and shells.
A sea otter has a pouch of loose skin under each arm to hold food and its favorite rock.
Sea otters eat sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels and fish.
Sea otters eat about a quarter of their body weight in food every day.
Some sea otters hold hands or wrap themselves in kelp while they sleep so they don't drift away.
A group of sea otters resting together in the water is called a raft.
Baby sea otters are called pups.
A mother sea otter carries her pup on her belly as she floats.
Sea otter pups are so fluffy that they float like little corks.
Sea otters can close their ears and nostrils when they dive.
Sea otters can hold their breath for about five minutes.
Sea otters have webbed back feet that work like flippers.
Sea otters help kelp forests by eating sea urchins, which would otherwise munch the kelp.
Healthy kelp forests are homes for many other ocean animals.
Sea otters are a 'keystone species,' which means their ocean home depends on them.
Long ago, sea otters were hunted for their fur until very few were left.
Today, sea otters are protected, and their numbers have grown in many places.
River otters are cousins of sea otters that live in rivers and lakes and spend more time on land.
faq: Why do sea otters hold hands?
Sea otters sometimes hold hands or wrap themselves in kelp while sleeping so they don't float away from each other.
How do sea otters stay warm?
Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal. It traps air next to their skin and keeps the cold water out.
What do sea otters eat?
Sea otters eat sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails and fish. They often use rocks to crack open hard shells.
What is the difference between a sea otter and a river otter?
Sea otters live in the ocean and float on their backs, while river otters live in fresh water and spend more time on land.

intro: Red foxes are clever, quick animals with fluffy tails and pointy ears. They live in forests, fields and even cities, and they can hear a mouse squeak from far away. Let's trot into some fun red fox facts!

quick.Home: Forests, grasslands, mountains, deserts and cities across North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa
quick.Food: Mice, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit and berries
quick.Size: About 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 m) long, including the tail
quick.Life span: About 2 to 5 years in the wild

facts: Red foxes live in more places around the world than almost any other wild meat-eating mammal.
Foxes are part of the dog family, along with wolves and coyotes.
Red foxes aren't always red. Some are black, silver or a mix called 'cross' foxes.
Most red foxes have a white tip on their bushy tails.
A fox's tail is called a brush.
Foxes wrap their fluffy tails around themselves like a blanket to stay warm.
A male fox is called a dog or a tod, and a female is called a vixen.
Baby foxes are called kits, cubs or pups.
Fox families live in dens, which are often underground burrows.
Red foxes have amazing hearing and can hear small animals moving under the snow.
In winter, foxes leap high into the air and pounce headfirst into the snow to catch mice.
Scientists think foxes may use Earth's magnetic field to aim their pounces.
Foxes are omnivores, so they eat both animals and plants.
Red foxes eat mice, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit and berries.
Foxes sometimes bury extra food to eat later. This is called caching.
Foxes have whiskers on their faces and legs to help them feel their way.
Red foxes can run about 30 miles per hour (48 km/h).
Foxes make lots of sounds, including barks, yips and even screams.
Foxes have vertical, slit-shaped pupils, a bit like a cat's.
Red foxes are mostly active at dusk, at night and at dawn.
Many red foxes have learned to live in big cities, like London.
Foxes usually hunt alone instead of in packs.
Fox parents both help raise their kits.
Fox kits start exploring outside the den when they are about a month old.
The arctic fox is a cousin of the red fox that turns white in winter.
faq: What do red foxes eat?
Red foxes are omnivores. They eat mice, voles, rabbits, birds and insects, plus fruit and berries.
Are foxes dogs or cats?
Foxes belong to the dog family, but they have some cat-like habits, like pouncing on prey and having slit-shaped pupils.
What is a baby fox called?
A baby fox is called a kit, cub or pup.
Why do foxes jump into the snow?
Foxes hear mice moving under the snow, then leap high and dive headfirst to catch them. This is called mousing.

intro: Squirrels are busy, bushy-tailed animals that scamper up trees, leap between branches and bury nuts for later. You can probably spot one in a park near you! Let's scurry into some super squirrel facts!

quick.Home: Forests, parks and cities on every continent except Australia and Antarctica
quick.Food: Nuts, seeds, acorns, fruit, mushrooms and buds
quick.Size: From about 3 inches to over 3 feet (1 m) long, depending on the kind

facts: There are more than 250 kinds of squirrels.
Squirrels live on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.
There are three main groups: tree squirrels, ground squirrels and flying squirrels.
Chipmunks, marmots and prairie dogs are all part of the squirrel family.
Squirrels are rodents, like mice and beavers.
A squirrel's front teeth never stop growing, so chewing nuts keeps them short.
Squirrels bury nuts and seeds to eat during winter.
A squirrel can bury thousands of nuts in a single season.
Squirrels use their great sense of smell, and their memory, to find buried food.
Forgotten nuts can grow into new trees, so squirrels help plant forests!
Some squirrels pretend to bury a nut to trick anyone who is watching.
Squirrels can turn their back feet around to climb down trees headfirst.
A squirrel's bushy tail helps it balance, keeps it warm and acts like an umbrella.
Squirrels flick their tails to send messages to other squirrels.
Flying squirrels don't really fly. They glide from tree to tree using flaps of skin.
Some flying squirrels can glide around 150 feet (45 m) in one leap.
Baby squirrels are called kits or kittens.
Squirrel nests in trees are called dreys, and they are made of twigs and leaves.
Squirrels can jump about 10 times the length of their bodies.
Squirrels have sharp claws that grip tree bark.
The African pygmy squirrel is tiny, only about 3 inches (7.5 cm) long without its tail.
The Indian giant squirrel can be over 3 feet (1 m) long, including its tail, and has colorful fur.
Ground squirrels live in underground tunnels.
Squirrels chatter, squeak and bark to warn each other about danger.
Squirrels are very good at solving puzzles to reach bird feeders!
faq: What do squirrels eat?
Squirrels mostly eat nuts, seeds, acorns, fruit, mushrooms and tree buds. Some also eat insects and eggs.
Why do squirrels bury nuts?
Squirrels bury food to save it for winter when food is hard to find. The nuts they forget can grow into new trees.
Can flying squirrels really fly?
No, flying squirrels glide. They stretch out flaps of skin between their legs and sail from tree to tree.
What is a squirrel's nest called?
A squirrel's nest in a tree is called a drey. It's made of twigs, leaves and moss.

intro: Ducks are water birds that quack, waddle and paddle around ponds and lakes. They have waterproof feathers and webbed feet that make them great swimmers. Let's paddle into some fun duck facts!

quick.Home: Ponds, lakes, rivers, marshes and coasts on every continent except Antarctica
quick.Food: Water plants, seeds, insects, snails and small fish
quick.Size: From about 12 inches to over 2 feet (30 to 70 cm) long
quick.Life span: About 5 to 10 years in the wild

facts: There are more than 100 kinds of ducks.
Ducks live on every continent except Antarctica.
A male duck is called a drake, and a female duck is called a hen.
Baby ducks are called ducklings.
Ducklings can swim soon after they hatch.
Ducklings follow the first moving thing they see, usually their mother. This is called imprinting.
Ducks have webbed feet that work like paddles.
Ducks have special oil glands near their tails to make their feathers waterproof.
Water rolls right off a duck's back, which is where the saying comes from!
Ducks' feet don't feel very cold because of special blood vessels that keep heat in.
Not all ducks quack. Many ducks whistle, coo, grunt or squeak.
Usually it's female mallards that make the loud 'quack' sound.
Dabbling ducks, like mallards, tip their bottoms up to eat plants under the water.
Diving ducks swim all the way underwater to find food.
Ducks eat water plants, seeds, insects, snails, worms and small fish.
Bread isn't good for ducks. Peas, corn and oats are healthier treats.
Male mallards have shiny green heads, while females are speckled brown.
The wood duck is one of the most colorful ducks in North America.
Wood duck ducklings jump out of tree nests, sometimes from high up, to reach the water!
Many ducks fly south in a V shape when the weather gets cold.
Ducks can sleep with one eye open to watch for danger.
Ducks have three eyelids.
Mother ducks line their nests with soft feathers from their own chests.
A group of ducks on the water is sometimes called a raft or a paddling.
Nursery rhymes love ducks, like the Five Little Ducks who went swimming one day!
faq: What is a baby duck called?
A baby duck is called a duckling. A male duck is a drake and a female duck is a hen.
Do all ducks quack?
No! Many ducks whistle, coo or grunt. The classic loud quack usually comes from female mallards.
What do ducks eat?
Ducks eat water plants, seeds, grass, insects, snails, worms and small fish. Bread isn't healthy for them.
Why don't ducks get wet?
Ducks spread oil from a gland near their tail over their feathers, which makes them waterproof.

intro: Sheep are fluffy farm animals famous for their soft, warm wool. They say 'baa,' stick together in flocks and have lived alongside people for thousands of years. Let's baa into some fun sheep facts!

quick.Home: Farms and grassy hills all over the world
quick.Food: Grass, clover, hay and other plants
quick.Size: About 4 to 6 feet (1.2 to 1.8 m) long

facts: A female sheep is called a ewe, a male sheep is called a ram, and a baby is called a lamb.
The word sheep is the same whether you mean one sheep or many sheep.
A group of sheep is called a flock.
There are more than 1,000 breeds of sheep.
People have raised sheep for about 10,000 years.
Sheep's wool keeps growing, so most farm sheep need a haircut called shearing once a year.
One sheep's wool can be made into several sweaters!
Wool is made of keratin, like your hair and nails.
Wool is naturally waterproof because of an oily substance called lanolin.
Lanolin is used to make some soaps and lotions.
Sheep are herbivores and eat grass, clover, hay and other plants.
Sheep have four parts to their stomachs, which helps them digest grass.
Sheep chew their food twice! They bring it back up and chew it again. This is called chewing the cud.
Sheep have rectangle-shaped pupils that help them see almost all the way around without turning their heads.
Sheep can recognize the faces of many other sheep and even people.
Sheep feel safer in a flock and follow each other closely.
Lambs can stand and walk within minutes of being born.
A mother sheep knows her lamb by its voice and smell.
Rams of some breeds have big, curly horns.
Bighorn sheep live wild in the mountains of North America and are great climbers.
Sheepdogs help farmers move flocks of sheep from place to place.
Sheep don't have top front teeth, just a hard pad on top.
Some sheep are raised for milk, which can be made into cheese like feta.
Sheep can be black, brown, white or spotted.
Sheep are stars of nursery rhymes, like Baa Baa Black Sheep and Mary Had a Little Lamb!
faq: What is a baby sheep called?
A baby sheep is called a lamb. A mother sheep is a ewe and a father sheep is a ram.
Why do sheep need to be sheared?
Most farm sheep grow wool all year and can't shed it on their own, so farmers give them a haircut called shearing to keep them cool and comfortable.
What do sheep eat?
Sheep are herbivores. They graze on grass and clover and eat hay in winter.
Are sheep smart?
Yes! Sheep can recognize dozens of faces, remember them for years and learn their way around.

intro: Camels are tough desert animals with humps on their backs and long eyelashes to keep sand out. They can go a long time without water and carry heavy loads across the hot desert. Let's trek into some fun camel facts!

quick.Home: Deserts and dry lands of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Australia
quick.Food: Desert plants, grass, leaves and even thorny shrubs
quick.Size: About 6 to 7 feet (1.8 to 2.1 m) tall at the hump

facts: There are two main kinds of camels: dromedaries with one hump and Bactrian camels with two humps.
A fun way to remember: a dromedary's hump makes a 'D' shape, and a Bactrian's two humps make a 'B' shape lying on its side.
Camel humps store fat, not water.
The fat in the hump gives camels energy when food is hard to find.
Camels can go a week or more without drinking water.
A very thirsty camel can drink about 100 liters (over 25 gallons) of water in a short time.
Camels have two rows of long eyelashes to keep sand out of their eyes.
Camels can close their nostrils to keep out blowing sand.
Camels have wide, padded feet that help them walk on soft sand without sinking.
Camels have thick pads on their knees so they can kneel on hot ground.
Camels' body temperature can change during the day to help them save water.
Camels eat thorny desert plants that most animals can't, thanks to their tough mouths.
A baby camel is called a calf.
Baby camels are born without humps.
Camels can carry heavy loads for long distances across the desert.
Camels have been called 'ships of the desert.'
Camels can run about 40 miles per hour (65 km/h) in short sprints.
Camels walk by moving both legs on one side of their body at the same time, which makes them sway.
Bactrian camels live in cold deserts and grow thick shaggy coats in winter.
Wild Bactrian camels are very rare and live in the Gobi Desert of China and Mongolia.
Camels grunt, moan and bellow to communicate.
Camel milk is a healthy drink for many people in desert countries.
There are many wild camels in Australia, brought there over 150 years ago.
Llamas and alpacas are cousins of camels from South America.
Alice the Camel from the song has five humps, but real camels only have one or two!
faq: Do camels store water in their humps?
No. Camel humps store fat, which the camel can use for energy. Camels can still go a long time without water because their bodies save it very well.
How many humps do camels have?
Dromedary camels have one hump and Bactrian camels have two humps.
How long can a camel go without water?
Camels can go a week or more without drinking, and even longer if they eat juicy plants.
What is a baby camel called?
A baby camel is called a calf. Calves are born without humps.

intro: Chickens are friendly farm birds that cluck, scratch and lay eggs. There are more chickens in the world than any other bird! Let's peck into some egg-cellent chicken facts!

quick.Home: Farms and backyards all over the world
quick.Food: Seeds, grains, bugs, worms and plants
quick.Size: Most are about 16 to 28 inches (40 to 70 cm) tall

facts: There are more chickens in the world than any other kind of bird.
A female chicken is called a hen, and a male chicken is called a rooster.
Baby chickens are called chicks.
Chickens came from a wild bird called the red junglefowl in Asia.
Chickens are distant relatives of dinosaurs, like the T. rex!
Hens can lay eggs without a rooster, but those eggs won't hatch into chicks.
Many hens lay about one egg a day.
Egg shells can be white, brown, blue or green, depending on the breed.
A chick takes about 21 days to hatch from its egg.
Chicks use a tiny bump on their beaks called an egg tooth to break out of the shell.
A mother hen clucks to her eggs, and the chicks can peep back from inside the shell.
Roosters crow in the morning, but they also crow at other times of the day.
Chickens can make dozens of different sounds to talk with each other.
Chickens have a 'pecking order,' which is a ranking of who is in charge of the flock.
Chickens can fly a little, but only short distances.
Chickens love dust baths! Rolling in dirt helps keep their feathers clean and bugs away.
Chickens are omnivores and eat seeds, grains, insects, worms and plants.
Chickens don't have teeth. They swallow small stones that help grind food in their gizzard.
Chickens can see more colors than people can.
Chickens can recognize many other chickens and people.
The red part on top of a chicken's head is called a comb.
The red flaps under a chicken's beak are called wattles.
Silkie chickens have fluffy feathers that feel like fur.
Some chickens like to be petted and can be very friendly pets.
Chickens sleep on perches called roosts and tuck their heads under their wings.
faq: What is a baby chicken called?
A baby chicken is called a chick. A mother chicken is a hen and a father chicken is a rooster.
How long does it take a chicken egg to hatch?
A chicken egg takes about 21 days to hatch when it is kept warm by a hen or an incubator.
Can chickens fly?
Chickens can fly a little, usually just short hops up onto fences or perches.
Are chickens related to dinosaurs?
Yes! Birds, including chickens, evolved from small feathered dinosaurs.
